history.note: Muslim-ruled Iberia (711–1492). Córdoba and Toledo became centers where Arabic, Latin and Hebrew learning met and was translated.
Under the Ptolemies (305–30 BCE) Alexandria's Library and Museum gathered scholars from across the Mediterranean.

name: Greenland Crossing
description: No cold penalties; +2 food on polar sea tiles.

history.note: Norse settlers and Thule Inuit shared Greenland from about 1200 to 1450; the Norse colonies vanished while the Inuit thrived.

name: Naukratis
description: +1 trade route; +2 gold in coastal settlements.

history.note: Naukratis in the Nile Delta, founded in the 7th century BCE, was Egypt's licensed port for Greek traders; Pharaoh Amasis (r. 570–526 BCE) made it their only base, and Greek and Egyptian gods had temples there.

From the 8th to 10th centuries Abbasid patrons paid translators, many of them Syriac-speaking Christians such as Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq, to put Aristotle, Galen, Euclid and Ptolemy into Arabic, preserving and extending them.
history.source: Dimitri Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture (1998)

name: Varangian Guard
description: Infantry +4 combat strength; an extra Warleader seat.

history.note: From about 988 the Byzantine emperors kept a bodyguard of Scandinavian and Rus' warriors armed with great axes; Harald Hardrada served in it. After 1066 many of its men were English.

name: Fānfāng of Guangzhou
description: +1 trade route; +20% gold in coastal settlements with a trade route.

history.note: By the Tang, Arab and Persian merchants lived in a foreign quarter (fānfāng) of Guangzhou under their own headmen. In 878 the rebel Huang Chao's army sacked the city and massacred many of its foreign traders.

Under the Yuan, the Mongol relay system (Mongol jam, Chinese zhan) ran over a thousand stations across China with horses, boats and carts for officials and envoys. Local households bore the heavy cost of supplying them.

name: Maragheh Observatory
description: +25% science in the capital; +20% thought great-people points.

history.note: In 1259, a year after his army sacked Baghdad and slaughtered much of its people, Hülegü founded an observatory at Maragheh under the Persian scholar al-Ṭūsī; al-ʿUrḍī of Damascus built its instruments.
